notes.definition: All materials in the living world are recycled to provide the building blocks for future organisms. Many materials, including carbon and water, cycle through the biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components of an ecosystem.
explanation: The Earth has a fixed amount of materials such as carbon, water and mineral ions. Living organisms take these materials from the environment to build their cells, and return them when they respire, excrete, die and decay. Because these materials are recycled, they are available again to provide the building blocks for future organisms. Many different materials cycle through both the abiotic parts of an ecosystem (air, water, soil, rocks) and the biotic parts (plants, animals and microorganisms).

In the carbon cycle, carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere by green plants and algae during photosynthesis. The carbon is used to make glucose, which is then turned into carbohydrates, fats and proteins that make up the body of the plant. When animals eat plants, some of this carbon becomes part of the animals' bodies. Carbon is returned to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide when plants, animals and microorganisms respire.

When plants and animals die, or produce waste such as faeces, microorganisms (decomposers such as bacteria and fungi) feed on the remains. As the decomposers respire, they release carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere, where it can be used again by plants for photosynthesis. Decomposers also release mineral ions (such as nitrates) from the dead material back into the soil, where they can be absorbed by plant roots. Without microorganisms, dead material would build up and the carbon and mineral ions in it would be locked away.

Some carbon becomes locked up for millions of years in fossil fuels (coal, oil and natural gas) when organisms die in conditions where decay cannot happen, such as waterlogged, oxygen-poor mud. When humans burn fossil fuels (combustion), this carbon is released quickly into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide. Burning wood also releases carbon dioxide. Increased combustion is raising the carbon dioxide concentration of the atmosphere.

The water cycle provides fresh water for plants and animals on land before it drains into the seas. Heat from the Sun causes water to evaporate from seas, lakes and rivers, and plants release water vapour from their leaves by transpiration. The water vapour rises, cools and condenses to form clouds. Water falls back to the ground as precipitation (rain, snow or hail). Some of this fresh water is taken up by plants through their roots and drunk by animals; the rest flows over the ground and through the soil into rivers and back to the sea. Water is continuously evaporated and precipitated.

The carbon and water cycles are vital to living organisms. The carbon cycle keeps carbon dioxide available for photosynthesis, which produces the food and oxygen that almost all other organisms depend on. The water cycle supplies the fresh water that land plants need for photosynthesis, support and transport, and that animals need to drink, as all chemical reactions in cells take place in solution. You do not need to learn the nitrogen cycle for GCSE AQA Biology.
keyFacts: All materials in the living world are recycled to provide building blocks for future organisms.
Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
Respiration by plants, animals and microorganisms returns carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
Combustion of fossil fuels and wood releases carbon dioxide.
Carbon passes from plants to animals by feeding.
Microorganisms (decomposers) break down dead organisms and waste, returning carbon dioxide to the air and mineral ions to the soil.
Water cycle: evaporation and transpiration, condensation, precipitation, then flow back to the sea.
The water cycle provides fresh water for plants and animals on land.
The nitrogen cycle is not required by AQA.

keyTerms.definition: The continuous movement of carbon between the atmosphere, living organisms, the oceans and fossil fuels.
The process in which plants and algae use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, removing carbon dioxide from the air.
The release of energy from glucose in living cells; aerobic respiration releases carbon dioxide.
Burning a fuel such as coal, oil, gas or wood, which releases carbon dioxide.
A microorganism (bacterium or fungus) that breaks down dead organisms and waste, releasing carbon dioxide and mineral ions.
The continuous movement of water by evaporation, transpiration, condensation and precipitation.
The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant, mainly through the stomata.
Water falling from clouds as rain, snow or hail.
Water vapour cooling and turning back into liquid water droplets, forming clouds.

workedExamples.title: Tracing a carbon atom
workedExamples.question: Describe how a carbon atom in carbon dioxide in the air could become part of a rabbit and then return to the air.
steps: A grass plant absorbs carbon dioxide and uses it in photosynthesis to make glucose.
The glucose is used to make carbohydrates, proteins or fats in the grass.
A rabbit eats the grass; the carbon compounds are digested, absorbed and used to build the rabbit's body.
The carbon returns to the air as carbon dioxide when the rabbit respires, or when the rabbit dies and decomposers feeding on it respire.
workedExamples.answer: Photosynthesis → carbon compounds in grass → feeding → carbon compounds in rabbit → respiration (by the rabbit or by decomposers) → carbon dioxide in air.

workedExamples.title: Explaining the role of decomposers
workedExamples.question: A gardener notices that leaves left on a lawn in autumn have disappeared by spring. Explain what has happened to the carbon and mineral ions in the leaves.
steps: Microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) and other decomposers fed on the leaves.
They digested the leaves and used the products in respiration.
Respiration released the carbon as carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Mineral ions from the leaves were released into the soil, where plant roots can absorb them.
workedExamples.answer: Decomposers broke the leaves down: the carbon was returned to the air as CO₂ by their respiration and mineral ions were returned to the soil.

workedExamples.title: Following water through the water cycle
workedExamples.question: Describe how water in the sea can become water in the cells of a tree.
steps: Heat from the Sun evaporates water from the sea, forming water vapour.
The vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds.
Water falls as precipitation (rain) over land.
Rainwater soaks into the soil and is absorbed by the tree's roots by osmosis.
workedExamples.answer: Evaporation → condensation → precipitation → absorption by roots.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think only animals respire and only plants photosynthesise, so plants do not release carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.right: In fact plants respire all the time, day and night, releasing carbon dioxide. During the day photosynthesis is usually faster than respiration, so there is a net uptake.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often forget that decomposers respire.
misconceptions.right: In fact decomposers return carbon to the air as carbon dioxide precisely because they respire as they feed on dead material.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think decomposers release carbon dioxide into the soil and mineral ions into the air.
misconceptions.right: In fact decomposers return carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide and mineral ions to the soil.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think water vapour forms clouds by evaporating.
misconceptions.right: In fact clouds form when water vapour cools and condenses into tiny droplets; evaporation is liquid turning into vapour.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think materials used by organisms are used up for ever.
misconceptions.right: In fact all materials are recycled; the same atoms are used over and over by future organisms.

realWorld: Composting garden and food waste uses decomposers to return mineral ions to the soil, reducing the need for artificial fertiliser.
Burning fossil fuels has increased atmospheric carbon dioxide from about 280 parts per million before the industrial revolution to over 420 parts per million today, contributing to global warming.
Deforestation reduces transpiration, so less water vapour enters the air and some regions receive less rainfall.
examTips: When describing the carbon cycle, name the process for each step: photosynthesis (removes CO₂), respiration and combustion (add CO₂), feeding (moves carbon to animals), decay by microorganisms.
When asked about the role of microorganisms, give both parts: they return carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide (by respiration) and mineral ions to the soil.
On carbon cycle diagrams, check the direction of arrows: arrows into the air are respiration or combustion; the arrow out of the air into plants is photosynthesis.
For the water cycle, use the precise terms: evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation.
Do not write about the nitrogen cycle: it is not on the AQA GCSE specification.
summary: All materials are recycled to provide building blocks for future organisms.
Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the air; respiration and combustion return it.
Feeding passes carbon compounds along food chains.
Decomposers return carbon to the air as CO₂ and mineral ions to the soil.
Water cycle: evaporation and transpiration → condensation → precipitation → back to the sea.
The water cycle provides fresh water for plants and animals on land.

flashcards.front: Why are materials recycled in the living world?
flashcards.back: To provide the building blocks for future organisms.

flashcards.front: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
Name two processes that return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
How does carbon pass from plants to animals?
flashcards.back: By feeding: animals eat plants and use the carbon compounds to build their bodies.

flashcards.front: What do decomposers return to the atmosphere?
What do decomposers return to the soil?
Name two groups of microorganisms that act as decomposers.
How are fossil fuels formed in the carbon cycle?
flashcards.back: Dead organisms that did not decay were compressed over millions of years into coal, oil and gas.

flashcards.front: Name the four main processes of the water cycle.
flashcards.back: Evaporation (and transpiration), condensation, precipitation, and flow back to the sea.
Loss of water vapour from plant leaves.

flashcards.front: Why is the water cycle important to living things?
flashcards.back: It provides fresh water on land for plants and animals before it drains into the sea.

flashcards.front: Why is the carbon cycle important?
flashcards.back: It keeps carbon dioxide available for photosynthesis, which provides food for nearly all organisms.
Yes, all the time; they release carbon dioxide day and night.

questions.question: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
markScheme: 1 mark: photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Green plants and algae take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. Respiration, combustion and decay all release carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which type of organism breaks down dead plants and animals?
markScheme: 1 mark: decomposers
questions.explanation: Decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, feed on dead material and waste. Producers make food by photosynthesis.

questions.question: In the water cycle, what is the name for water falling from clouds as rain or snow?
markScheme: 1 mark: precipitation
questions.explanation: Precipitation is water falling as rain, snow or hail. Condensation forms the clouds, and evaporation and transpiration put water vapour into the air.

questions.question: What is transpiration?
options: Loss of water vapour from the leaves of plants
markScheme: 1 mark: loss of water vapour from the leaves of plants
questions.explanation: Transpiration is evaporation of water from leaves, mostly through stomata. It adds water vapour to the atmosphere.

questions.question: Which organisms release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by respiration?
markScheme: 1 mark: plants, animals and microorganisms
questions.explanation: All living organisms respire, including plants and decomposers. Forgetting that plants respire is a common error.

questions.question: What do microorganisms return to the soil when they decompose dead material?
markScheme: 1 mark: mineral ions
questions.explanation: Decomposers return mineral ions to the soil and carbon dioxide to the atmosphere. Glucose is used up by the decomposers in respiration.

questions.question: How does carbon in a plant become part of a caterpillar?
markScheme: 1 mark: by feeding
questions.explanation: The caterpillar eats the plant, digests the carbon compounds and uses them to build its own body.

questions.question:
Dead plants have built up in a peat bog over thousands of years without decaying.
Table 1 compares the conditions in the peat bog with the soil in a nearby woodland.
What is the most likely reason the dead plants in the bog have not decayed?
options: There is too much oxygen in the waterlogged soil
The waterlogged, acidic conditions have little oxygen, so decomposers cannot respire aerobically and work very slowly
There is too much light for decomposers
Plants in bogs do not contain carbon
markScheme: 1 mark: the waterlogged, acidic conditions have little oxygen, so decomposers cannot respire aerobically and work very slowly
questions.explanation: Water fills the air spaces in the soil, so oxygen is low, and the acidity also inhibits microorganisms. Decay is very slow, so carbon remains locked in the peat.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air in a dense forest over 24 hours on a sunny day.
Which explanation for the pattern is correct?
options: Plants only respire during the day
In the day photosynthesis is faster than respiration; at night only respiration occurs
Decomposers stop respiring during the day
markScheme: 1 mark: in the day photosynthesis is faster than respiration; at night only respiration occurs
questions.explanation: Respiration happens all the time in all organisms. In light, photosynthesis removes CO₂ faster than respiration adds it; in the dark there is no photosynthesis, so CO₂ builds up.

questions.question: Which process in the carbon cycle releases carbon that was locked up in fossil fuels?
markScheme: 1 mark: combustion
questions.explanation: Burning (combustion) of coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide. Precipitation is part of the water cycle.

questions.question: In the water cycle, which process forms clouds?
markScheme: 1 mark: condensation
questions.explanation: Water vapour rises, cools and condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds. Evaporation and transpiration produce the vapour in the first place.

markScheme: 1 mark: A: photosynthesis
1 mark: B: combustion (allow burning)
questions.explanation: Arrow A takes carbon dioxide out of the air into green plants, so it is photosynthesis. Arrow B releases carbon dioxide from fossil fuels into the air, so it is combustion. The other arrows into the air are respiration by plants, animals and decomposers.

questions.question: Name two types of microorganism that act as decomposers.
markScheme: 1 mark: bacteria
1 mark: fungi
questions.explanation: Bacteria and fungi are the main microorganisms that decompose dead material.

questions.question: Explain the role of microorganisms in cycling materials through an ecosystem.
acceptedAnswers: return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere
return mineral ions to the soil
markScheme: 1 mark: they break down (decompose) dead organisms and waste and release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere through respiration
1 mark: they return mineral ions to the soil
questions.explanation: Both parts are needed: carbon to the atmosphere as CO₂, and mineral ions to the soil.

questions.question: Explain why the water cycle is important for organisms that live on land.
markScheme: 1 mark: it provides fresh water on land (through precipitation) before it drains into the sea
1 mark: plants need water for photosynthesis or support, and animals need water to drink / chemical reactions happen in solution
questions.explanation: Sea water is too salty for most land organisms. The water cycle turns it into fresh water and delivers it to land as rain.

questions.question: Describe how carbon in the body of a dead rabbit is returned to the atmosphere.
markScheme: 1 mark: decomposers (bacteria and fungi) feed on / digest the dead rabbit
1 mark: they use the carbon compounds in respiration
1 mark: releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere
questions.explanation: The key link is that decomposers respire, which is what releases the carbon as CO₂.

questions.question: Suggest what would happen to plants in an ecosystem if all the decomposers were removed. Explain your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: dead organisms and waste would build up / not decay
1 mark: mineral ions would not be returned to the soil, so plants would lack them (for example nitrate for proteins)
1 mark: less carbon dioxide would be returned to the air for photosynthesis, so plant growth would decrease
questions.explanation: Decomposers recycle both mineral ions and carbon. Without them, these materials stay locked in dead material and plants are starved of them.

questions.question: Explain how a large-scale increase in burning fossil fuels and cutting down forests affects the carbon cycle.
markScheme: 1 mark: combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide (carbon locked up for millions of years)
1 mark: fewer trees means less photosynthesis, so less carbon dioxide is removed (and burning or decay of trees releases more)
1 mark: so the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere increases
questions.explanation: Both changes shift the balance: more CO₂ is added and less is removed, so atmospheric CO₂ rises.

questions.question: Name the process by which water from the sea enters the atmosphere.
markScheme: 1 mark: evaporation
questions.explanation: Heat from the Sun evaporates sea water, forming water vapour; the salt is left behind.

questions.question: Explain how carbon from carbon dioxide in the air becomes part of the protein in a plant.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis to make glucose
1 mark: glucose is used (with nitrate ions) to make amino acids, which form proteins
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis traps carbon in glucose, which is then converted into other carbon compounds such as proteins, starch, cellulose and lipids.

questions.explanation: Process B is the loss of water vapour from the leaves of the tree into the air, which is transpiration. Process A is evaporation from the sea and process C is precipitation.

questions.question: Explain how plants contribute to the water cycle.
markScheme: 1 mark: plants absorb water from the soil through their roots
1 mark: water vapour is lost from the leaves by transpiration into the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Plants move water from the soil into the air, adding to the water vapour that later condenses and falls as precipitation.

questions.question: A gardener puts grass cuttings on a compost heap. Explain why the compost later helps plants to grow.
markScheme: 1 mark: decomposers break down the grass, releasing mineral ions (such as nitrate) into the compost
1 mark: plants absorb the mineral ions through their roots and use them for growth (for example nitrate to make proteins)
questions.explanation: Compost works as a natural fertiliser because decomposers recycle the mineral ions locked up in dead plant material.

options: The plant does not need carbon dioxide or mineral ions
Carbon and mineral ions are recycled by photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition inside the bottle
The plant makes new carbon atoms by photosynthesis
Water leaves the bottle and is replaced from outside
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon and mineral ions are recycled by photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition inside the bottle
questions.explanation: In a closed system the same materials cycle: CO₂ from respiration is used in photosynthesis, and decomposers return mineral ions from dead leaves. Atoms are not created, and water cycles inside the bottle too.

questions.question: Name the gas that plants absorb from the air for photosynthesis.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is taken in through the stomata and used to make glucose.

markScheme: Indicative content: carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is absorbed by green plants and algae in photosynthesis; it is used to make glucose and then carbohydrates, fats and proteins; animals eat plants (feeding) so carbon passes along food chains; plants, animals and decomposers respire, releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere; when plants and animals die or produce waste, decomposers (bacteria and fungi) feed on them; decomposers respire, returning carbon dioxide to the atmosphere; some dead organisms do not decay and are compressed over millions of years into fossil fuels; combustion of fossil fuels (and wood) releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically sequenced description of photosynthesis, feeding, respiration (including by decomposers), decay and combustion of fossil fuels.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes most processes correctly but with some omissions, for example missing fossil fuels or decomposer respiration.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names one or two processes with little description.
questions.explanation: Name the process for every transfer, and make sure arrows into the atmosphere are respiration or combustion, while the arrow out of the atmosphere is photosynthesis.

questions.question: Describe the water cycle and explain why it is important to living organisms.
markScheme: Indicative content: water evaporates from seas, lakes and rivers using heat from the Sun; plants lose water vapour by transpiration; water vapour rises, cools and condenses to form clouds; water falls as precipitation (rain, snow); it provides fresh water on land; plants absorb water through their roots; animals drink it; water flows back to the sea through rivers and soil; water is continuously evaporated and precipitated; importance: fresh water needed for photosynthesis, transport and support in plants, and for reactions in cells, which happen in solution.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct sequence of evaporation (and transpiration), condensation and precipitation, with a clear explanation of importance to organisms.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names some stages or gives a simple statement of importance.
questions.explanation: Use the correct process names in order, then link the cycle to fresh water supply on land for plants and animals.

questions.question:
A tree in a woodland dies and falls to the ground. Over 10 years the trunk is completely broken down.
Explain how the carbon and mineral ions in the tree are recycled, and how this benefits other organisms in the woodland.
markScheme: Indicative content: decomposers (bacteria and fungi) feed on the dead wood; they secrete enzymes to digest it and absorb the products; decomposers use the carbon compounds in respiration; respiration releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere; this carbon dioxide is absorbed by other plants for photosynthesis; photosynthesis produces glucose used for growth; mineral ions (for example nitrate, magnesium) are released into the soil; these are absorbed by roots of other plants; nitrate used to make proteins, magnesium for chlorophyll; more plant growth provides food and shelter for animals; animals (detritivores such as woodlice) feeding on the wood are food for other animals; materials provide building blocks for future organisms.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed explanation covering decomposition and respiration releasing CO₂, release of mineral ions to the soil, and clear links to growth of plants and benefits to other organisms.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains the role of decomposers in returning carbon or mineral ions, with some links to other organisms.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as 'the tree rots' or 'bacteria break it down'.
questions.explanation: Top answers give the mechanism (decomposers digest and respire), both products (CO₂ to air and mineral ions to soil), and how other organisms use them.
